headline: When every library gets its hand-written best-practice — static class plus inline style for the changing value — they reach parity with next-yak's css-var, which is the point: next-yak compiles that split as a feature, the others earn it by developer discipline on each dynamic value.

microbench.why: Given the hand-written workaround — a static class with the dynamic value pushed onto an inline `style` — `cnfast`, `vanilla` and `tailwind-merge` regenerate no class and land within 2% of the css-prop lane; even `styled-components` recovers via `.attrs`, sidestepping its own `generateAndInjectStyles`. That parity is the finding: it is what next-yak's css-var does automatically. The developer reaches it here by manually splitting static from dynamic, per component, every time; the styled lane trails the workarounds (0.833M) only because it still wraps a `Yak`, while the css-prop fold emits the plain element the hand-written versions write by hand.

autocannon.why: Under load the hand-tuned workarounds and the css-prop fold all clear ~1240-1270 req/s because no request regenerates a class. `emotion` (403 req/s) and `panda` (298 req/s) lack an inline-style escape and still serialize per element per request.

attribution.why: With the value on an inline style, the library slice nearly vanishes for the workaround lanes — `cnfast` 0.079 ms, `styled-components` 0.487 ms via `.attrs`, `vanilla` 0 — so the SSR split is almost pure react-dom. The css-prop fold matches them at 0.106 ms lib. The styled lane's 0.426 ms lib is the `Yak` wrapper that survives a dynamic value (which compiles to a css-var and blocks the fold), and `panda`'s style-props still cost 2.43 ms of component self-time.

hydrate.why: One dynamic value keeps hydration cheap for everyone with a static sheet; the runtime libraries stay closer to the pack here than in the static cases because a single inline value regenerates little — `styled-components` 86.1 ms, `goober` 78.5 ms, well under their 150-250 ms on repeated static classes.

inp.why: Updating a single element's value is cheap for every lane (~7-8 ms, inside the interaction spread) — an inline-style write or a css-var write costs the same, so the field is a tie. Only `panda` (13.0 ms) stays back, re-running its style-prop serializer on the re-render.

mount.why: Cold mount tracks render size: the css-prop fold and hand-written lanes mount at ~60-65 ms; the runtime libraries add only a modest first-inject here (`styled-components` 84.0 ms, `emotion` 89.1 ms) because there is a single dynamic rule, not a thousand.

renderTiming.why: One style recalc for every approach — the css-var write and the inline-style write recalc identically, so the paint path is parity. The styleMs spread is sub-millisecond (0.093-0.146 ms).

payload.why: next-yak ships one static class plus inline var values (5.24-6.32 kB gz). The workaround lanes carry their class strings plus the inline styles (`tailwind-merge` 15.8 kB, `cnfast` 16.8 kB), and the runtime libraries their bundle plus rules (`styled-components` 18.7 kB, `emotion` 18.1 kB).

nsweep.why: At 4000 elements the hand-written workarounds and the css-prop fold stay flat with react-dom (~2.6-2.8 ms). The styled lane's `Yak` wrapper compounds to 4.91 ms, and the libraries without an inline escape rise — `emotion` 9.78 ms, `panda` 11.3 ms.

crossCase: `dyn-fair` sits between `dyn-translate` and `dyn-inline` above. It is the idiomatic middle: the naive class-per-value cost from `dyn-translate` disappears once a developer hand-splits static class from inline value, and the whole field converges near `dyn-inline`'s plain-inline-style floor. The delta that matters is not a number but a cost of ownership — parity here is a build-time optimization done by hand, per component, forever; next-yak's css-var ships it once as a feature, which is why its styled and css-prop lanes read the same across all three cases while the others need the discipline.
